blocks.text: Most interesting questions in data and in AI involve more than one uncertain quantity at once, whether a model rains tomorrow and whether traffic is heavy, or which word came before and which word comes next in a sentence. Joint probability is the tool that describes two or more random quantities together, in a single distribution, rather than treating each one in isolation.

blocks.alt: A joint distribution over two variables producing marginals and an independence check
blocks.caption: From a joint distribution to marginals and an independence check

blocks.text: 1. What Joint Probability Means

Joint probability is the probability that two events happen together, written P(A and B), or equivalently P(A, B) using the comma notation introduced in the probability rules lesson. Instead of asking about A alone or B alone, a joint probability answers a question about both at once.

For example, if A is the event a customer is browsing on mobile and B is the event a customer completes a purchase, P(A and B) is the probability a randomly chosen customer is both on mobile and completing a purchase, a single number that captures the overlap between the two events directly.

code.content: p_mobile_and_purchase = 0.18   # 18 percent of all customers are both on mobile and purchasing

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: If A is a patient having a fever and B is a patient having a positive flu test, P(A and B) equal to 0.12 means that out of every 100 patients seen, 12 have both a fever and a positive flu test at the same time, a single number blending both conditions together.

blocks.text: 2. From Single Events to Random Variables

The probability rules lesson worked mostly with single named events like rain or spam. Joint probability is usually described more generally in terms of random variables, quantities whose value is not yet known but which follow a probability distribution over their possible outcomes, covered in full in the discrete and continuous random variable lessons later in this module.
A joint distribution simply extends this idea to two random variables at once, X and Y, describing how likely every possible pair of values (x, y) is, rather than describing each variable separately.

A useful mental shortcut is that a single event, like rain, can always be viewed as a random variable with just two outcomes, rain and no rain, so every rule that applies to joint distributions over random variables also applies to the simpler joint probability of two named events covered in section 1.
3. The Joint Probability Table

When both variables take a small number of discrete values, the cleanest way to represent a joint distribution is a table, sometimes called a joint probability matrix, with one variable along the rows and the other along the columns, and every cell holding P(X equals that row value and Y equals that column value).

Every cell in this table is a joint probability, for instance the top left cell says P(Cold and Rain) equals 0.20. Because the table covers every combination of the two variables with no overlap, every cell in the entire table must sum to exactly 1, a direct extension of the sum-to-1 rule from the probability rules lesson.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.20, 0.15],
                   [0.10, 0.55]])
assert np.isclose(joint.sum(), 1.0)   # the whole table must sum to 1

blocks.text: 3.1 Reading Rows Versus Columns

By convention the row variable is read first and the column variable second, so a table with temperature as rows and rain as columns is read as P(temperature and rain), with the temperature value named first and the rain value named second in each cell reference.

This convention is not universal across every textbook or paper, so whenever a joint table appears without an explicit label, it is worth checking which variable was used for rows and which for columns before reading off any specific cell value.
4. Marginal Probability: Summing Out a Variable

Marginal probability is the probability of a single variable, recovered from a joint table by summing across the other variable. To get P(X equals Cold) from the table above, add up every cell in the Cold row, 0.20 plus 0.15, giving 0.35. The name comes from the old habit of writing these row and column sums in the margins of a printed table.

Marginalizing works in either direction, summing across rows collapses out the column variable and leaves the marginal distribution of the row variable, while summing down columns collapses out the row variable and leaves the marginal distribution of the column variable.

code.content:
p_cold = joint[0, :].sum()   # 0.35, marginal probability of Cold, summing out rain/no-rain
p_rain = joint[:, 0].sum()   # 0.30, marginal probability of Rain, summing out cold/warm
print(p_cold, p_rain)

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: From the weather table, the marginal probability of Rain is 0.20 plus 0.10, which is 0.30, meaning it rains 30 percent of the time overall, regardless of temperature. Notice this single number throws away the temperature information entirely, that tradeoff is exactly what marginalizing means.

blocks.text: The word marginal can feel counterintuitive at first since it describes a probability that ignores information, but the name is purely historical, referring to where the row and column totals were physically written on paper, not to any sense of the result being unimportant.

code.content:
p_warm = joint[1, :].sum()    # 0.65, marginal probability of Warm
p_no_rain = joint[:, 1].sum()  # 0.70, marginal probability of No Rain
print(p_warm, p_no_rain)

blocks.text: 5. Joint Probability and Independence

Two variables are independent exactly when every joint probability factors cleanly into the product of the two marginals, P(X and Y) equals P(X) times P(Y), for every possible pair of values. This is the multiplication rule from the probability rules lesson, applied to every cell of the joint table at once.

The independence lesson elsewhere in this module covers this condition in much greater depth, including how to formally test for it and why it matters so much for simplifying calculations, but the quick check below is enough to catch dependence in a small table.

code.content:
p_cold, p_rain = 0.35, 0.30
expected_if_independent = p_cold * p_rain   # 0.105
actual = joint[0, 0]                        # 0.20
print(actual, expected_if_independent)      # not equal, so cold and rain are not independent

blocks.text: Testing independence this way only confirms it for the single cell being checked, a fully rigorous check needs every cell in the table to match its expected value under independence, which is exactly the more formal test the independence lesson in this module walks through in full.
6. Reading a Joint Distribution as a Heatmap

A joint probability table over two discrete variables is naturally visualized as a small grid of shaded cells, darker shading for higher probability, which makes it easy to spot at a glance which combinations of values are common and which are rare.

blocks.alt: Heatmap of the weather joint probability table
blocks.caption: Darker shading marks the most probable Warm and No Rain combination

blocks.text: For joint distributions with more than two or three discrete values per variable, a heatmap becomes far more useful than a plain table, since the eye can spot a bright cluster of high probability mass much faster than it can scan a large grid of numbers.
7. Joint Probability in Code

Building and querying a joint distribution in code is usually as simple as constructing a small array or dictionary keyed by the pair of variable values, then summing along an axis whenever a marginal is needed.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.20, 0.15],
                   [0.10, 0.55]])
marginal_temp = joint.sum(axis=1)   # [0.35, 0.65], summing out rain
marginal_rain = joint.sum(axis=0)   # [0.30, 0.70], summing out temperature
print(marginal_temp, marginal_rain)

blocks.text: The axis argument controls which variable gets summed out, axis 1 collapses across columns leaving one value per row, while axis 0 collapses across rows leaving one value per column, a detail worth double-checking any time a marginal comes out looking wrong.

Real datasets rarely arrive as a neatly pre-built joint table, more often a joint distribution has to be estimated first by counting how often each combination of values occurs in a large sample, then dividing every count by the total number of observations.

code.content:
raw_counts = np.array([[20, 15],
                        [10, 55]])
joint_estimated = raw_counts / raw_counts.sum()
print(joint_estimated)   # matches the weather table from section 3

blocks.text: 8. More Than Two Variables

Nothing about joint probability is limited to exactly two variables, a joint distribution can just as well describe three, four, or hundreds of variables together, though a full table becomes exponentially larger and harder to write out as more variables are added.

With three discrete variables X, Y, and Z, the joint probability P(X, Y, Z) still sums to 1 across every combination of values, and any single variable or pair of variables can still be recovered by marginalizing out the rest.

For three binary variables, device type, purchase outcome, and returning customer status, the full joint table would need 8 entries, one for every combination of the three variables, all still summing to exactly 1, illustrating how quickly a joint table grows as more variables are added.
9. Joint Probability with Continuous Variables

When one or both variables are continuous rather than discrete, the joint probability table becomes a joint probability density function, a surface over the plane of possible (x, y) pairs rather than a finite grid of cells, and marginalizing becomes an integral instead of a sum.

The mechanics carry over directly though, the joint density still integrates to 1 over the whole plane, and integrating out one variable still recovers the marginal density of the other, exactly mirroring the discrete case covered above.

A common example is a joint density over height and weight in a population, a continuous surface where the volume under the surface over any region gives the probability a randomly chosen person falls within that combined height and weight range.

The variational autoencoder and diffusion model lessons elsewhere in this curriculum both lean on this continuous joint density picture directly, treating a learned latent variable and an observed input as two jointly distributed continuous quantities.
10. Joint Probability in AI Practice

Joint distributions over multiple model outputs show up constantly in applied machine learning. A multi-label classifier that predicts both a topic and a sentiment for a document is implicitly working with a joint distribution over those two output variables, and checking whether they are independent or correlated is often a genuinely useful diagnostic.

items: Co-occurrence matrices in natural language processing count how often pairs of words appear near each other, and normalizing such a matrix turns it directly into a joint probability table over word pairs.

Generative models that output multiple correlated fields at once, such as an image caption model predicting several attributes together, are implicitly learning a joint distribution over those attributes rather than several unrelated ones.
Recommendation systems often model the joint probability that a user both views and clicks an item, since the marginal view probability alone hides which items convert into clicks once seen.

blocks.text: Whenever a model is described as outputting a distribution over pairs, triples, or larger tuples of quantities, a joint distribution is precisely what is being modeled underneath the description.

Diffusion and other generative image models effectively learn an enormous joint distribution over every pixel value in an image at once, sampling from that learned joint distribution is precisely what produces a coherent generated image rather than a grid of unrelated random pixel values.
11. Joint Probability Versus Conditional Probability

Joint probability P(A and B) and conditional probability P(A given B) are closely related but answer different questions, joint probability describes both events happening out of every possibility, while conditional probability describes A happening within the narrower world where B is already known to have happened.

The two are linked by P(A and B) equals P(A given B) times P(B), a relationship the conditional probability lesson in this module builds on directly, and which is also the starting point for deriving Bayes theorem.

code.content:
p_b = 0.30                 # P(rain)
p_a_given_b = 0.667        # P(cold given rain), read off the table
p_a_and_b = p_a_given_b * p_b
print(round(p_a_and_b, 2))  # 0.20, matches the joint table cell directly

blocks.text: A quick way to keep the two straight is that joint probability answers how likely a specific combination is out of everything possible, while conditional probability answers how likely one part is, once the rest is already known to be true.
12. A Worked Example
An online store tracks two variables for each visitor, device type, either mobile or desktop, and outcome, either purchase or no purchase. Historical data gives the following joint probability table.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.18, 0.42],
                   [0.12, 0.28]])
assert np.isclose(joint.sum(), 1.0)
p_mobile = joint[0, :].sum()          # 0.60, marginal probability of mobile
p_purchase = joint[:, 0].sum()        # 0.30, marginal probability of purchase
expected_if_independent = p_mobile * p_purchase   # 0.18
print(p_mobile, p_purchase, expected_if_independent)

blocks.text: The expected joint probability under independence, 0.18, matches the actual observed joint probability of mobile and purchase exactly, 0.18, meaning device type and purchase outcome behave independently in this particular dataset, an outcome worth double-checking against a larger sample before relying on it.

blocks.title: Double-checking the marginals
blocks.content: Adding the mobile marginal of 0.60 and the desktop marginal of 0.40 gives exactly 1, and adding the purchase marginal of 0.30 and the no-purchase marginal of 0.70 also gives exactly 1, a fast sanity check worth running on any joint table before trusting further calculations built on it.

blocks.text: 13. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing a marginal probability with a joint probability, reading a row or column sum as if it described a single specific cell rather than the whole row or column.
Forgetting that an entire joint table, not just one row, must sum to exactly 1, and failing to catch a construction error that leaves probability mass missing or double counted.
Assuming two variables are independent without checking, and applying the plain multiplication rule to a joint probability that actually needs the full table or a conditional probability instead.
Marginalizing along the wrong axis in code, accidentally summing out the variable meant to be kept rather than the one meant to be removed.
Treating a joint probability density value as though it were itself a probability, an issue covered in full detail in the continuous random variables lesson later in this module.

blocks.text: A subtler version of the independence mistake is checking only one cell of a joint table against the independence formula and declaring the whole table independent, when a single matching cell is not enough evidence on its own.
14. Practice: Build and Query a Joint Table

A survey records two variables for each respondent, favorite season, either summer or winter, and preferred drink, either hot or cold, giving the joint probability table below. Compute both marginal distributions and check whether the two variables are independent.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.05, 0.45],
                   [0.35, 0.15]])
marginal_season = joint.sum(axis=1)   # marginal of summer/winter
marginal_drink = joint.sum(axis=0)    # marginal of hot/cold
expected_summer_hot = marginal_season[0] * marginal_drink[0]
print(marginal_season, marginal_drink, expected_summer_hot)

blocks.text: Compare the computed expected_summer_hot value against the actual table cell of 0.05, a large mismatch between the two is a clear sign season and drink preference are dependent, exactly the pattern intuition would predict.

As an extra check, verify that both marginal distributions computed above individually sum to 1, marginal_season should sum to 1 and marginal_drink should sum to 1, confirming no probability mass was lost or duplicated while marginalizing.

Marginal probability and joint probability are two sides of the same table, one describing the whole combined picture and the other describing a single variable extracted from it, a distinction worth keeping sharp before moving on to conditional probability.
Key Takeaway

Joint probability describes two or more variables together in a single distribution, rather than describing each one in isolation, and a joint probability table or density is the object that makes questions about combinations of outcomes answerable directly.

Marginal probability recovers a single variable distribution by summing, or integrating, the joint distribution over every value of the other variables, an operation used constantly whenever only part of a joint distribution is actually needed. Independence, conditional probability, and Bayes theorem, covered elsewhere in this module, all build directly on the joint distribution ideas introduced here.
